cards.back: Disease-causing organism: bacteria, viruses, fungi or protozoa.
Barrier defences: skin, mucous membranes and their secretions — stop pathogens entering.

cards.front: How does blood clotting defend the body?
cards.back: Platelets + clotting factors → thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin mesh → seals the wound and blocks pathogen entry.
Innate immune cell that engulfs and digests pathogens. Neutrophils are fast and short-lived; macrophages are larger and longer-lived.
Histamine → vasodilation + leaky capillaries → redness, heat, swelling and pain. Brings more immune cells to the infection site.

cards.front: Why does a fever help against infection?
cards.back: Higher temperature inhibits pathogen reproduction and increases immune cell activity. Only moderate fevers help — very high fevers are dangerous.
Differentiate into plasma cells (secrete antibodies) and memory cells (long-term immunity).
Short-lived B-lymphocyte derivative — an antibody factory secreting thousands of identical antibodies per second.
Y-shaped: 2 heavy + 2 light chains. Variable regions at the tips bind ONE antigen (2 binding sites); constant region determines class.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary immune response — the graph?
cards.back: Primary: slow rise, lower peak, short duration. Secondary: memory cells → faster rise, higher peak, longer duration. Label the lag phase in both.
Antigens without causing disease: attenuated (weakened), inactivated, subunit or mRNA forms. Result = artificial active immunity + memory.
When most of the population is immune, transmission chains break — even unvaccinated individuals are protected. Threshold depends on the disease's R₀.

cards.front: Why DON'T antibiotics work on viruses?
cards.back: Viruses lack the bacterial targets (cell wall, bacterial ribosomes, DNA gyrase) that antibiotics attack.
Antibiotics create selection pressure: resistant bacteria survive, reproduce and pass resistance genes (often on plasmids) → resistant population.
Complete prescribed courses; never use antibiotics for viral infections; hygiene to limit spread; reduced livestock use. Any one, explained.
Identical antibodies from a hybridoma — a B lymphocyte fused with a myeloma cell: divides forever AND secretes one specific antibody.
Antibodies specific to hCG carry a coloured marker on the strip — hCG in urine binds and produces the visible line.
Retrovirus: reverse transcriptase copies RNA → DNA, integrated into the host genome. Destroys helper T cells → adaptive immunity collapses → AIDS.
Allergy: overreaction to a HARMLESS antigen (histamine from mast cells). Autoimmune: attack on the body's OWN cells (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis).
Passive: ready-made antibodies (breast milk, injection) — immediate but temporary, no memory. Active: own response + memory cells — lasting.
